title: Methods for In Vivo Biomechanical Testing on Brachial Plexus in Neonatal Piglets
protocol: Quarantine 1–2 day-old piglets for at least 24 h after arrival.
House piglets in clean and sanitized stainless-steel cages on aspen chip bedding.
Feed piglets ad libitum with pig milk replacer.
Maintain the room temperature at 85 °F to ensure a thermo-neutral environment.
Remove feed from piglets 2 hours prior to the experiment.
Inject piglets with an intramuscular injection of ketamine and xylazine.
Transport piglets via transport cage to the surgical space.
Administer 4% isoflurane inhalation anesthetic mixed in oxygen by nose cone.
Confirm that the animal is deeply anesthetized by assessing the absence of palpebral and withdrawal reflexes.
Place the animal in the supine position for intubation.
Use a laryngoscope to guide the intubation tube into the trachea.
Secure the intubation tube once placed in the trachea.
Place the animal on the ventilator after securing the intubation tube.
Provide piglets with a mix of isoflurane, oxygen, and nitrous oxide for maintenance anesthesia.
Administer fentanyl to ensure continued adequate depth of analgesia and sedation.
Continue giving a dose of fentanyl every 1–2 hours.
Establish intravenous (IV) access in the subcutaneous abdominal vein or any other peripheral vein.
Establish the arterial line through the femoral artery.
Monitor the depth of anesthesia by confirming the absence of canthal reflex and absence of withdrawal response to toe pinch.

Perform continuous monitoring of physiological parameters during anesthesia and throughout the experiment, which includes arterial blood pressure, electrocardiography (ECG), end-tidal CO2, pulse oximetry, and body temperature.
Monitor blood gases and blood sugars every 0.5–1 h.
Give intravenous fluids (50% dextrose and 50% normal saline) to animals anesthetized longer than 1 h at ~100 cc/kg/day as needed to ensure euglycemia.
Provide analgesia and/or increase inhalant anesthesia as needed.
Maintain the animal at normal oxygen tension by controlling ventilator parameters and drug dosages.
Place the animal on a temperature-regulated circulating water blanket such that normal body temperature is maintained at 39 °C for the duration of the experiment.
Place the animal in a supine position on the operating table after proper anesthesia as described in section 3, with the upper limb in abduction, exposing the axillary region.
Cover the animal with a surgical drape.
Make a midline incision over the skin and fascia using a #10 blade, extending from the trachea down to the upper third of the sternum.
Extend the incision horizontally on each side from the suprasternal notch along the edge of the clavicle to the upper arm using forceps and hemostat.
Release superior and inferior flaps by blunt dissection with scissors and forceps, providing access to cervical and thoracic regions of the brachial plexus.
Identify axis (C2) and first rib at T1.
Locate lower three cervical (C6–C8) and first thoracic (T1) spinal vertebral foramen using identified landmarks.
Examine the plexus carefully to locate bifurcations of divisions, forming an M shape.
Label brachial plexus regions above these bifurcations closer to the spine as root/trunk.
Label those below these bifurcations as chord followed by nerve, located closer to the arm.
Attach the electromechanical actuator onto the base using large C-clamps.
Attach the 200 N load cell to the actuator.
Screw in a clamp to the load cell that consists of padded plexiglass.
Attach a camera to a tripod.
Connect USB cables from the camera, actuator, and load cell to the computer.
Plug the computer, actuator, and load cell into a power source.
Calibrate the load cell prior to recording applied loads.
Set the actuator at a 90° angle using an adjustable handle and checking with a protractor.
Open the software that works with the load cell.
Press the Start button to show a live readout of voltage.
Hang weights from the clamp ranging from 0–1,000 g in increments of 100 g and record measured voltages.
Calculate the linear equation of voltages and weights by finding the slope (m) and intercept (b).
Insert the calculated linear equation into the mechanical set-up code.
Cut the BP nerve using fine scissors.
Clamp the cut side of the BP nerve in the custom-built clamp.
Manually place black acrylic paint or India ink on the clamped BP segment.
Place a calibration grid flat within the animal.
Use the camera's software to view the camera's placement directly over the tested segments.

Record initial measurements such as the height at which the nerve inserts into the body from the table and the height of the clamp from the table, the angle of the actuator, and the full length of the tissue.
Open the programming software containing the graphical user interface (GUI).
Run the GUI by pressing the Run button.
Initialize the system by pressing the Initialize button.
Tare the system by pressing the Tare button.
Stretch the BP segment by pressing the start test button.
Record the failure site, which is the point at which the tissue ruptures.
Euthanize piglets at the end of the experiment with a lethal dose of pentobarbital (120 mg/kg i.v.).
Open the video file from the experiment within the motion tracking software by selecting File | Open Video File.

Use the calibration grid to setup the scale in the motion tracking software using the Line tool, right-clicking on the line after it is drawn, selecting Calibrate Measure, and entering a known value in centimeters.

Track the markers on the tissue within the motion tracking software by right-clicking on the video and selecting Track Path and aligning the center of the marker with the marker on the tissue and tacking it until rupture.
Export the x- and y-coordinates from the markers by selecting File Export to Spreadsheet.
Import the data into a programming software.
Calculate the distance between x- and y-coordinates over time to calculate strain values.
Divide the change in distance by the original distance after accounting for changes in inclination during stretch.
Determine strain values between each pair of adjacent markers at each timepoint.
Calculate the average of these strain values.
